goal: Show other aircraft SimConnect knows about (AI traffic) as live markers on the existing live map, alongside the user's own aircraft. agent/agent.js gains a second, independent SimConnect request (requestDataOnSimObjectType / simObjectDataByType) that collects in-range aircraft and pushes them to the server as a batch over the existing HTTP ingest channel; the server holds them in memory keyed by SimConnect object id, prunes them when they go stale or leave range, and exposes them to the client on the existing REST poll; client/src/components/LiveMap.tsx renders one visually distinct marker per traffic aircraft, added, moved and removed as the polls arrive. Nothing about traffic is written to flights.db, and the existing single-aircraft SimFrame -> flightManager -> flights.db pipeline is left byte-for-byte equivalent in behaviour.
frozen_decisions: User's request, verbatim: "gather the AI traffic information from simconnect and display it on the live map."
No persistence. Traffic is not written to `flights.db`. It's live-view only, matching "display... on the live map," not "log."
Follow the existing agent-only architecture. No new server-side SimConnect connection; same-machine mode is not addressed by this run (it doesn't exist today for the user's own aircraft either).

Reuse the poll/REST model as the default; the Designer evaluates whether traffic volume/churn justifies a separate polling endpoint (`/api/traffic`) vs. folding into `/api/status`, and whether the existing 1s/3s cadence is adequate or traffic needs its own (probably coarser) interval given dozens of objects can be in range at once.
Zero regression to the existing single-aircraft flight-logging pipeline (SimFrame -> flightManager state machine -> flights.db). Traffic is additive, on a separate data definition/request id.
No new runtime dependency on server, client or agent. node-simconnect ^4.1.1 is already the agent's only dependency and gains no version change.

DevOps / Ship step is skipped for this run: no build, packaging, deploy, Docker or env-provisioning change is involved. `npm run build` and the existing start path are unchanged. If a Dispatcher believes it needs a dependency, a script or a Dockerfile change, that is an escalation, not a decision it makes.
sequencing_rationale: The contract is frozen before any code, because four components (agent, ingest, in-memory store, client map) all encode the same traffic record shape and the same staleness rule, and three of them are written by different cold agents. A contract discovered by the third implementer is three rewrites.

The server and client land before the agent, deliberately inverting the data flow. The agent is the one layer that cannot be executed on this machine (Linux, no MSFS, node-simconnect not installed and not installable to any useful effect), so it must be the last thing added and the only remaining unknown when it is. By then the endpoint it posts to is already proven with synthetic batches.

Phase 2 therefore ships something real without the sim: `curl` a synthetic traffic batch at a scratch server and watch markers appear, move and expire on the live map. That is also the fixture path that makes phase 3 falsifiable — the agent's batch assembly is proved by feeding its own output to the server that phase 2 built.

Escape hatches ship before the automation they protect: the server-side batch size cap, the malformed-batch rejection and the prune timer are all in phase 2, before phase 3 turns on an agent that can push dozens of objects a second. The agent-side kill switch ships in the same task as the gathering it disables, because an opt-out that arrives after the thing it opts out of is not an opt-out.

The risky logic is isolated into two pure modules with their own CLI inspectors — `src/traffic.ts` (keying, staleness, prune, caps) and `agent/traffic.js` (batch assembly, own-aircraft and ground filtering, dedupe) — so both are falsifiable with `node` alone, with no sim, no browser and no test framework. `agent/traffic.js` in particular must not import node-simconnect, or it stops being runnable on this machine.

Traffic state lives in a new `src/traffic.ts` store, not inside `src/flightManager.ts`. flightManager is the flight-logging state machine that writes flights.db; the strongest available guarantee of criterion 4 (zero regression) is that this run does not edit that file at all, and the plan gives no task permission to.

File ownership is assigned so no two tasks ever touch the same file. Server-side traffic types live in `src/traffic.ts` (owned by T-003); the client's mirror of them lives in `client/src/types.ts` (owned by T-004); `README.md` is owned only by T-006, the last task to land, which documents the finished feature end to end rather than three tasks editing one file.

T-004 depends on T-003 rather than running beside it, even though their paths are disjoint. The client's acceptance criteria are end-to-end (seed a scratch server, count markers in a real browser), and that evidence does not exist until the endpoint does. The parallelism would have bought wall-clock and cost the only honest check the client task has.

phases.name: Freeze the traffic contract
phases.ships: A reviewed, frozen design.md: the traffic record's exact fields and units, the ingest endpoint and batch shape with its limits, the keying/staleness/prune rule, the client-visible response shape and its backward-compatibility guarantee, the marker distinction, and a worked example plus truth tables the implementers' inspectors transcribe. After this phase nobody downstream has to invent a field name.

phases.name: Server store, ingest and map rendering — provable with synthetic traffic
phases.ships: With no sim and no agent, the user can POST a synthetic traffic batch to the server and see one distinct marker per aircraft on the live map next to their own, watch them move on the next batch, and watch them vanish when a batch drops them or goes stale. Malformed and oversized batches are rejected instead of accepted. With no traffic posted at all, the app behaves exactly as it does today.

phases.name: Agent-side gathering — real traffic from the sim
phases.ships: The Windows agent pulls in-range AI aircraft from SimConnect on its own request id and pushes them to the server, so the live map shows real traffic during a flight. An env-var opt-out turns it off without touching code, and the README says what it does, what it costs and that none of it is logged.

tasks.title: Freeze the AI-traffic data contract end to end
tasks.goal:
Write design.md for this run and freeze every decision the three implementation tasks would otherwise each invent. Resolve the intake's open questions and nothing beyond them. The design is the single source of truth for field names, units, ids, limits and timings; it is quoted, not paraphrased, by every task after it.

The intake (.claude/runs/2026-09-08-ai-traffic-map/intake.md) has the verified facts about the current pipeline — do not re-derive them, but do open agent/agent.js, src/ingest.ts, src/server.ts's /api/status handler and client/src/components/LiveMap.tsx to fit the contract to the code as written.

STRUCTURE IS PART OF THE DELIVERABLE. .claude/tools/ctx.sh slices design.md by numbered heading, so downstream tasks can only be given cheap context if the headings are exactly `## <n>. Title` and `### <n>.<m> Title`, numbered as follows:
  1. Overview and data flow
  2. Traffic record — the wire shape: every field, its type, its unit, whether it is optional, and what the client does when it is absent
  3. Agent-side gathering — data definition id and request id (both distinct from DEF_FLIGHT_DATA=0 / REQ_FLIGHT_DATA=0), the SimConnect variables and their order, the radius in metres and whether it is configurable, the re-request cadence (requestDataOnSimObjectType is a one-shot request, not a periodic subscription — confirm this against node-simconnect 4.1.1 and state the consequence), which SimObjectType is asked for, how the user's own aircraft is excluded from the result, whether ground/parked aircraft are filtered, and the env-var opt-out's exact name and semantics
  4. Ingest contract — endpoint path, HTTP method, batch payload shape, the maximum number of objects in one batch and what the server does when that is exceeded, the exact 400 responses for each way a batch can be malformed, and whether x-ingest-token applies (it must, for consistency with /api/ingest/frame)
  5. Server state and pruning — what the record is keyed by, when an object is considered stale, when it is pruned, what happens to an object present in one batch and absent from the next, the hard cap on retained objects, and the server-side kill switch
  6. Client-visible API — whether traffic rides on GET /api/status or a separate endpoint, and either way the exact response shape, the poll cadence, and an explicit backwards-compatibility guarantee: what /api/status returns when no traffic has ever been posted, and why that is indistinguishable from today's response to an old client
  7. Client rendering — how a traffic marker differs from the user's own (the ✈ divIcon is currently 24px with a drop-shadow and a heading-90 rotation; say exactly what changes), marker add/update/remove lifecycle, whether the map ever auto-pans or zooms to traffic (it must not), and what happens to markers when the poll fails or the agent disconnects
  8. Worked example — one concrete batch JSON as the agent would post it, and the exact JSON the client-visible API returns for it. Implementers copy this verbatim into their curl commands
  9. Truth tables — the rows src/inspect-traffic.ts and agent/inspect-traffic.js transcribe by hand: staleness/prune cases (fresh, aged past the window, dropped from a later batch, re-appearing after a gap, over the cap, empty batch) and agent batch-assembly cases (user's own object, duplicate object id within one sweep, missing/NaN coordinates, ground object if filtered, opt-out enabled)
  10. Must-not-change — the invariants of the existing pipeline this run may not touch: src/flightManager.ts is not edited, POST /api/ingest/frame's contract is unchanged, the simObjectData handler still ignores every requestID except REQ_FLIGHT_DATA, the /api/status keys that exist today keep their names/types/absence semantics, and nothing traffic-related reaches flights.db

Bias the contract towards the smallest thing that satisfies the goal: lat/lon/altitude/heading is enough to draw a marker. Only add a field if section 7 actually renders it.

tasks.title: Review the agent changes and the run's end-to-end coherence
tasks.goal: Gate phase 3 and the run. This review carries more weight than a normal one because the code under it cannot be executed here: the only place a mistake surfaces is the user's sim, mid-flight, on the same SimConnect handle that logs their real flights. Read agent/agent.js's full diff as a careful reader of the SimConnect API, not as a runner of commands. Judge specifically: could the traffic request, its handler, or its timer perturb the existing frame path in any way — shared ids, shared buffers, a handler that reads the wrong number of fields from the buffer and desyncs, an exception escaping into the SimConnect event loop, an interval that keeps the process alive after 'quit'/'close', or a reconnect that registers the traffic timer twice? Then check the whole run for coherence: agent record shape == ingest validator == store == API == marker, and the READMEs against what the code now does.
acceptance_criteria: The three `node --check`s and `node agent/inspect-traffic.js` are re-run by the reviewer with transcripts, and at least two truth-table rows are traced by hand from design.md §9 through agent/traffic.js's code.
The reviewer reproduces the agent-output -> server round trip itself on its own scratch server and its own copy of flights.db, and reports the status codes and response body it saw.

Cross-layer field trace done end to end for the full run and reported as a table: SimConnect variable -> agent record field -> POST body field -> store field -> API response field -> marker property. Any name or unit that changes without a §2 mapping is request_changes.

The four success criteria in intake.md are each answered with the evidence that satisfies them, and criterion 4 (zero regression) is backed by `git diff --stat` for the whole run showing src/flightManager.ts, src/db.ts and every migration path untouched, and no package.json changed anywhere.

README.md and agent/README.md are checked against the code as written — every env var, default, radius and cadence they state is verified against the source, and a wrong number in the README is request_changes, not a nit.

Live-system safety: the user's server on port 3000 still answers `curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/status`, the live flights.db md5 is unchanged for the whole run, and `git status --porcelain` shows no stray scratch files outside .claude/runs/.
The review closes with the residual risk list for the user's first flight with this on: what to watch for, and how to turn it off (the opt-out env var, quoted from the README).
